concepts.name: Functional versus architectural analogy
concepts.summary: The paper's stated limit on its own claim: the J-space matches many of the functional properties global workspace theory assigns to the workspace, while sharing only some of its architectural ones.
concepts.explanation: Global workspace theory makes two kinds of claim. The functional claims concern what conscious access does — report, top-down control, deliberate reasoning, flexible generalization, selectivity. The architectural claims concern how the brain implements it — specialized, encapsulated processors competing for entry to a workspace that broadcasts back to them through recurrent connections. The paper designed its experiments against the functional claims, and states that it does not claim language models reproduce the architecture. Several architectural features are said to have no clean analog in a transformer: there are no obviously separable input processors, and the broadcast the paper documents occurs within a single feedforward pass rather than through recurrent loops. The paper reports some degree of competition for access to the J-space, but says it is unclear whether this mirrors the sharp competitive ignition that characterizes workspace entry in the brain. Section 9.4 states the same limit more sharply: the analogy is weakest in implementation, and the paper says it does not know whether that difference matters for any of the theory's functional predictions.

concepts.name: Recurrent cortical broadcast
concepts.summary: In the brain, broadcast is held to be carried by recurrent loops and long-range cortical connections. This is the part of global workspace theory with no direct counterpart in a transformer's forward pass.
concepts.explanation: Global workspace theory as developed by Dehaene and colleagues attaches broadcast to a physical story: long-range connections between cortical areas, together with recurrent feedback that sustains and amplifies a representation once it has won entry. The paper identifies this mechanism as the point where its analogy is weakest. A standard transformer has no recurrence within a forward pass, so the broadcast the paper documents runs across layers in a single sweep. The paper says it does not know whether depth in a transformer plays a role similar enough to recurrence in a brain to enable the same functionality. Section 9.3 draws one consequence: recurrent dynamics allow a human workspace to hold and elaborate a thought over an indefinite number of processing cycles, whereas a model that needs deliberation beyond its feedforward depth must externalize it, writing intermediate results into the context as tokens and reading them back at later positions.

citedFrom.refText: Dehaene, Stanislas and Kerszberg, Michel and Changeux, Jean-Pierre. A neuronal model of a global workspace in effortful cognitive tasks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper names recurrent loops and long-range cortical connections as the theory's broadcast mechanism but does not describe the neuronal model itself; that model is set out in the cited work.

concepts.name: Separable input processors
concepts.summary: The brain-side picture has distinct input systems whose outputs compete for the workspace. The paper notes that a transformer has no obviously separable processors of this kind.
concepts.explanation: In the architectural half of global workspace theory, the workspace is fed by identifiable, largely encapsulated processors that run in parallel and compete for entry. The paper states that a transformer offers no obvious counterpart: there are no obviously separable input processors to compete. This is one of the features it lists when declining to claim that language models reproduce the theory's architecture. The paper does report some degree of competition for access to the J-space, but does not attribute that competition to distinct upstream modules.

concepts.name: Convergence on a workspace
concepts.summary: The paper's reading of its own result: nothing in the transformer imposes a workspace, so finding one suggests that learning systems converge on this organization under the right computational pressures.
concepts.explanation: Section 1.2 gives the prior argument for why a language model might develop a workspace without being built with one: a common representational format is likely computationally useful, since an intermediate result can be written once and read by many processes, and a model that must chain reasoning steps, apply general operations in arbitrary contexts, and answer questions about its own processing stands to benefit. The paper contrasts this with architectural proposals that install a workspace-like bottleneck into a network by design. Section 9.3 reports that the workspace already appears in the pretrained base model, so next-token prediction alone is sufficient to induce it. The Outlook states the conclusion: that such a structure exists at all in language models suggests the functional architecture associated with conscious access is not an accident of biological implementation, but a solution that learning systems converge on when faced with the right computational pressures. The claim is offered as a suggestion drawn from one family of models; the paper reports no comparison across architectures or training objectives that would test convergence directly.
